method: Topics whose evidence lists research citations (paper titles, journals, years, author names) instead of observable criteria. Each citation line is replaced with observable, child-level criteria grounded in the topic's description and assessmentPrompt. `before` keeps the original citation text. Applied by scripts/apply-evidence-rewrites.mjs.

rewrites.name: Author's word choices
before: collaborative multilayered text interpretation in 5-8 year olds
after: Point out a word or phrase an author chose and say how it made them feel or what it made them picture
Suggest a different word the author could have used and explain how it would change the effect
Explain that authors choose words, order, and tone on purpose to affect the reader

rewrites.name: Inference vs Explicit Meaning
before: inference vs literal comprehension development research
online inference making and comprehension monitoring (PMC 2021)
after: Point to the words in a text that state a fact directly
Identify something they worked out from clues that the text does not say outright
Sort statements about a text into "the text says" and "I figured out", and explain the clues behind each inference

rewrites.name: Knowing What You Don't Know
before: word consciousness and vocabulary metacognition research
after: Sort words from a text into "know well", "half-know", and "don't know"
Notice a half-known word while reading and say what they think it means and how sure they are
Check an uncertain word by using context, a dictionary, or asking, then say whether their guess was right

rewrites.name: Monitoring Comprehension
after: Notice and say when they have read a sentence or paragraph without understanding it
Stop and reread, ask a question, or look at a picture when meaning breaks down
Explain the difference between saying the words and understanding what they mean

rewrites.name: Reading for Meaning
before: reading comprehension research on comprehension-decoding separation
after: Tell in their own words what a short text they just read or heard was about
Say "I read it but I don't know what it means" when they can say the words but not explain them
Explain that reading means understanding the words, not just saying them correctly

rewrites.name: Reflecting on Your Language Use
after: Describe how they speak or write differently for two audiences (e.g., a friend vs. a teacher) and give examples
Explain why a change in audience or purpose calls for different words, tone, or formality
Name one part of their reading, writing, or speaking they want to improve and how they plan to work on it

rewrites.name: Reviewing Own Writing
after: State the effect they wanted their writing to have on a reader (e.g., make them laugh, persuade them)
Reread their own writing and point to a part that does or does not achieve that effect
Change a sentence or section to make it work better for the reader, not only to fix spelling or punctuation

rewrites.name: Checking Sources Against Each Other
before: Historical Thinking in the Elementary Years (ERIC)
after: Compare two sources about the same event and list facts they agree on and facts they disagree on
Explain why checking more than one source gives a better picture than trusting just one
Suggest a reason two sources might disagree and what other evidence could settle it

rewrites.name: Different Accounts of the Same Event
before: Initiating Historical Thinking in Elementary Schools
after: Retell two different accounts of the same event and say how they differ
Explain that two people can both be honest and still describe an event differently
Suggest a reason two accounts differ (e.g., where each person was or what they cared about)

rewrites.name: Evidence from the Past
before: Historical Thinking in the Elementary Years (ERIC)
after: Answer "How do we know?" about a past event by naming a kind of evidence (an object, building, picture, document, or story)
Sort objects or pictures into things from long ago and things from today, and explain the clues
Explain that people learn about the past from things that survived or were left behind

rewrites.name: Evidence Versus Interpretation
before: Development of historical understanding among 9-14 year olds
Ways of Seeing: Evidence and Learning in the History Classroom (RRCHNM)
after: Sort statements about a historical topic into evidence (what survived) and interpretation (what someone argues from it)
Explain how two historians could reach different conclusions from the same evidence
Support their own interpretation of a past event with specific pieces of evidence

rewrites.name: Questioning Historical Sources
before: Teaching Historical Thinking Using Primary Sources (Library of Congress)
after: Ask who made a source, when, and why before using it
Explain how a creator's purpose or point of view might affect what a source shows or leaves out
Decide whether a source is more or less trustworthy for a given question, and explain why

rewrites.name: Understanding People in Their Own Time
after: Explain why people in a past time might have thought a practice was normal, using what life was like then
Describe how a past action looks different when judged by today's values and by the values of its own time
Avoid calling people in the past "stupid" or "bad" without first considering the beliefs and knowledge of their time

rewrites.name: Asking for Help
after: Try a task on their own before asking for help
Ask for help when still stuck, saying what they tried and where they got stuck
Ask for help calmly instead of giving up or getting upset

rewrites.name: Connecting New & Old Ideas
after: Connect a new idea to something they already know (e.g., "That's like...")
Explain how a new idea is similar to and different from something learned before
Use what they already know to make sense of a new example

rewrites.name: Feeling of not understanding
after: Say when something they are reading or hearing does not make sense, instead of carrying on
Point to the word, sentence, or step that confused them
Ask a question or reread when they notice they are confused

rewrites.name: Finding Knowledge Gaps
after: Rate their understanding of each part of a topic as solid, shaky, or not yet, with honest reasons
Test themselves on a part they think they know and check whether they really do
Make a plan to work on the parts they rated shaky or not yet

rewrites.name: Learning from Mistakes
after: Look back at a wrong answer and explain what went wrong
Tell whether a mistake came from misunderstanding, missing a step, or carelessness
Correct the mistake and say what they will do differently next time

rewrites.name: Reflecting After Learning
after: After finishing a project or topic, describe what helped them learn most
Name something that was confusing and what they did about it
Say one thing they would do differently next time and why

rewrites.name: Thinking Before Starting
after: Before starting a new topic or task, tell what they already know about it
Ask themselves what they want to find out before they begin
Use something they already know to help start a new task (e.g., "This is like the problem we did yesterday")

rewrites.name: Transferring Skills
after: Name a skill or strategy from one subject that could help in another (e.g., using a chart in science and in writing)
Use a strategy learned in one situation to solve a problem in a new one
Explain why a strategy works in both places

rewrites.name: Feelings Versus Actions
before: Effects of Age and Gender in Emotion Regulation (PMC 2020)
after: Explain that they can feel angry, scared, or jealous without having to act on it right away
Describe something they could do while having a strong feeling instead of hitting, yelling, or grabbing
Use a calming step, such as taking a breath or walking away, before acting on a strong feeling

rewrites.name: Naming Your Feelings
before: Fostering Emotional Literacy in Young Children (HeadStart.gov)
after: Name the feeling they are having (e.g., happy, sad, angry, scared, excited, frustrated)
Match feeling words to faces, pictures, or story characters
Say how their body feels with a strong emotion (e.g., "My tummy feels tight when I'm nervous")

rewrites.name: Patterns in Your Own Reactions
before: middle childhood self-reliance in emotion regulation
after: Describe a situation that often triggers a strong feeling for them (e.g., being tired, left out, or put on the spot)
Notice a pattern in their own reactions (e.g., "I get grumpy when I'm hungry")
Suggest a way to plan ahead for a situation they know is hard for them

rewrites.name: Personal Growth Over Time
before: emotion vocabulary development continues to age 11 (PMC)
after: Name something that used to be hard for them and is easier now
Explain what helped them change, such as practice, help from others, or a new strategy
Describe something that is hard now that they expect to get better at, and how

rewrites.name: Changing Your Mind with Evidence
before: hypothesis testing and argumentation from evidence in young children
after: Compare their prediction with the result and say whether it matched
Accept a result that does not match their prediction instead of insisting the experiment went wrong
Change their explanation to fit new evidence and explain what made them change their mind

rewrites.name: Correlation vs Causation
before: developmental changes in children's recognition of evidence relevance to causal explanations
after: Explain that two things happening together does not prove that one causes the other
Suggest another reason two things might happen together (e.g., a third factor)
Describe a fair test that could show whether one thing really causes the other

rewrites.name: Could there be another explanation?
before: prompts to consider alternative possible worlds research (6-7 year olds)
after: Give at least one other possible explanation for a result they observed
Suggest how they could test which explanation is right
Explain why the first explanation that fits is not always the correct one

rewrites.name: Observation vs Interpretation
before: observation vs interpretation in primary science
BERA: children's observation skills in nature
after: Describe what they actually saw, heard, or measured in a science activity
Sort statements into observations ("the ice melted") and interpretations ("the ice melted because of the heat")
Point to the observation that supports an interpretation
